questions.q: In the dice lab, what shape does the histogram of the **sum** of $n = 2$ dice have?
questions.explain: There are 6 ways to roll a 7 but only one way to roll 2 or 12, so the counts rise and fall linearly — a triangle. With more dice it becomes more bell-shaped.

questions.q: One die has standard deviation $\sigma \approx 1.71$. What is the standard deviation of the **mean** of $n = 4$ dice?
questions.explain: The SD of the mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 1.71/2 \approx 0.85$. Dividing by $n$ instead of $\sqrt{n}$ gives $0.43$; $3.42 = \sigma\sqrt{n}$ is the SD of the *sum*.

questions.q: Which statement about the Central Limit Theorem is correct?
options: Under suitable conditions (independence, finite variance), the distribution of sample means approaches a Normal as $n$ grows — even if the data are not Normal
It says every dataset is Normally distributed
It only works when the original data are Normal
$n > 30$ always guarantees an exact Normal distribution
questions.explain: The CLT concerns sums/means, not the raw data. $n > 30$ is only a rough guide — skewed or heavy-tailed populations may need more, and the result is always an approximation.

questions.q: How does the CLT show up in stochastic gradient descent?
options: It makes every mini-batch gradient exactly equal to the full gradient
It forces the loss to be Normally distributed
The mini-batch average gradient is approximately Normal, centered on the true full-batch gradient (for large enough batches)
It removes the need for a learning rate
questions.explain: A mini-batch gradient is an average of per-example gradients, so by the CLT it is roughly Normal around the true gradient, with spread shrinking like $1/\sqrt{\text{batch size}}$.
